title: A City Without Walls: The Measuring Line
summary: In the third night vision Zechariah sees a young man going out to measure Jerusalem, and an angel sends word that the city will be too full of people and animals to be held by walls, because the LORD himself will be a wall of fire around it and its glory within. A call follows for the exiles still in Babylon to flee and come home, with the promise that God is coming to dwell in Zion and that many nations will join themselves to him.
story: The first two visions (1:7-21) told the people that God would return to Jerusalem and break the powers that had scattered them. This vision turns to the city itself. The builders are working on a temple in a small, half-empty town with broken walls, and the question is what Jerusalem will be. The answer is larger than anyone expected: a city overflowing past its borders, protected by God himself. The chapter then turns outward to the Jews still living in Babylon, and further, to the nations. It sets up themes the rest of the book returns to, above all God dwelling among his people and the nations coming to him (8:20-23; 14:16).
historical: When this vision came, around February 519 BC, Jerusalem's walls had lain in ruins since the Babylonians broke them down in 587 or 586 BC (2 Kings 25:10). They would not be rebuilt until Nehemiah's governorship, around 445 BC, some seventy-five years later (Nehemiah 1 to 6). The population was small. Many families had chosen to stay in Babylon, where Jewish communities had settled in during the exile and some had prospered. The call to flee from the land of the north (verse 6) is addressed to them. Babylon lay east of Judah, but armies and travelers from Mesopotamia reached Judah by the road that ran up the Euphrates and down through Syria, so the prophets often speak of invasion and exile as coming from the north (Jeremiah 1:14). Babylon itself had fallen to Cyrus in 539 BC, and, according to Persian and Babylonian records, rose in revolt against Darius in 522 and 521 BC, so it was no permanent home.
cultural:
Ancient cities were defined by their walls. A city without walls was either a village or a ruin, and it was defenseless; walls meant safety, identity, and a limit on how many could live inside. The Hebrew word in verse 4 for a city without walls is the word for open country villages, settlements that spread across the land because they had no enclosure. Zechariah turns the image upside down: Jerusalem will be unwalled not because it is weak but because it is too full, and it will need no walls because God is its wall.

The wall of fire and the glory within recall the exodus, when the LORD went before Israel in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night (Exodus 13:21-22) and his glory filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34). The phrase the Daughter of Zion, common in the prophets, personifies the city and its people as a young woman, often in a tender or protective sense. The apple of the eye (verse 8) is the pupil, the most sensitive and carefully guarded part of the body; the same image appears in Deuteronomy 32:10 and Psalm 17:8. In verse 12 God calls Judah his portion, using the language of an inheritance of land, and the phrase the Holy Land appears here for the only time in the Old Testament.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1-5 are the third vision, built like the others on seeing, asking, and an angel's answer, though here the answer is delivered at a run to the young man with the line. Verses 6-13 are a poetic oracle attached to the vision, with urgent commands (get up, escape, shout for joy, be silent) and a speaker who shifts in a puzzling way between God and one sent by God. Four times the speaker says that the LORD of Hosts has sent me (verses 8, 9, 11, and in 4:9 again), so the messenger's authority is part of the message. The chapter ends with a call to all people to be silent before God, a liturgical line like Habakkuk 2:20 and Zephaniah 1:7, marking the solemn moment when God rises to act. In the Hebrew Bible these verses are numbered 2:5-17.

outline.t: Third vision: the man with the measuring line
Flee from Babylon, for God will judge the plunderers
I am coming to dwell among you, and many nations will join

doctrines.note: God does not merely protect the city from outside; he promises to be the glory within it and to dwell among his people. His presence, not stone walls, is what makes Jerusalem secure.

Many nations will join themselves to the LORD and become his people (verse 11). The promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed through him is renewed in a small, struggling community, and the language of my people is extended beyond Israel.
Those who plundered God's people touched the apple of his eye. God will turn their own servants against them. His care for his people includes accountability for those who harm them.

words.note: Shakan, to dwell or settle. It is the verb behind the word for the tabernacle (mishkan, the dwelling place) and later Jewish talk of the Shekinah, God's dwelling presence. Verses 10 and 11 twice promise that God will dwell in the midst of his people.

Perazah, open country or unwalled villages. It describes settlements without fortifications. Verse 4 uses it to say that Jerusalem will be an open city, spilling beyond any wall because of the number of its people and animals.

Lavah, to join or attach oneself. The same verb is used in Isaiah 56:3 and 6 of foreigners who join themselves to the LORD. In verse 11 whole nations join him and become his people, one of the Old Testament's widest visions of Gentile inclusion.

Kavod, glory, the weighty presence and honor of God. God promises to be the glory within Jerusalem (verse 5), and verse 8 speaks of the LORD sending the messenger after glory, a phrase whose exact sense is debated.

christ: The chapter's central promise, I am coming to dwell among you (verse 10), is taken up in the New Testament with deliberate echoes. John says that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), using a Greek verb connected with the tabernacle. Revelation's picture of the new Jerusalem draws on the same hope: God's dwelling is with men, a city whose gates are never shut and whose light is the glory of God (Revelation 21:3, 23-25). The promise that many nations will join themselves to the LORD and become his people is the hope Paul sees realized as Gentiles are brought into God's people through Christ (Ephesians 2:11-22). The puzzling voice of one whom the LORD of Hosts has sent, who speaks with God's own authority, has been read by many Christian interpreters as pointing toward the Son sent by the Father, though others take it as the prophet himself; the text leaves it open.

hard.q: Who is speaking when the text says the LORD of Hosts has sent me?
hard.a: Verses 8-11 are hard to follow because the speaker seems to be both the LORD and someone the LORD has sent. There are three main readings. Many scholars take the speaker as Zechariah himself: the prophet quotes God's words, then adds that when these things happen the people will know God sent him, a claim he makes again in 4:9 and 6:15. Others take the speaker as the angel of the LORD, who throughout the visions speaks for God and yet is distinguished from him. Many Christian interpreters, noticing that the one sent speaks as God and promises to dwell among the people, have read the passage as a hint of the Son sent by the Father. The grammar allows each reading. The phrase in verse 8, rendered by the BSB as after His Glory has sent Me, is also uncertain in Hebrew and is translated in several different ways.

questions: Jerusalem's safety would come from God's presence rather than from walls. What walls do you rely on that God might want to replace with himself?
Many exiles had settled comfortably in Babylon. What might God be calling you to leave in order to come home?
God says whoever touches his people touches the apple of his eye. How does that change the way you see those who belong to him, including people you struggle with?
